title: Faith That Overcomes and the Assurance of Life
summary: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, loves God's children, and keeps his commands, and this faith overcomes the world. Jesus came by water and blood, and the Spirit, the water, and the blood testify together. God's testimony is that eternal life is in his Son, and John writes so that believers may know they have it. The letter closes with confidence in prayer, a word about sin that leads to death, three great statements of what we know, and a final warning against idols.
story: This last chapter gathers the letter's threads. Belief, love, and obedience, the three tests John has been circling, are shown to be one: to believe in Jesus is to be born of God, to be born of God is to love his children, and to love God is to keep his commands. The chapter then answers the question the letter has been building toward, how believers can be sure. John states his purpose plainly in verse 13, matching the purpose statement of his Gospel (John 20:31). The letter began with the Word of life; it ends with the Son who is the true God and eternal life.
historical:
The phrase water and blood (verse 6) is best understood against the teaching of John's opponents. If they held, like Cerinthus as Irenaeus describes him, that the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism but left before his death, they would affirm that Christ came by water (the baptism) but deny that he came by blood (the cross). John insists: not by water alone, but by water and blood. The same Son of God who was baptized also died. Other interpreters connect the water and blood with the flow of blood and water from Jesus' side at the crucifixion (John 19:34), or with the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper.

Verses 7-8 carry a famous textual note. Older English Bibles, such as the King James Version, read at this point that there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one. This wording, called the Johannine comma, is absent from the early Greek manuscripts and from the early translations other than Latin. It first appears in Latin writings of the late fourth century and later entered manuscripts of the Latin Vulgate. It appears in only a handful of late Greek manuscripts, some of them in the margin. Erasmus left it out of the first two editions of his printed Greek New Testament (1516 and 1519) and included it in the third (1522), from which it passed into the Textus Receptus and the King James Version. Nearly all modern translations omit it, as the BSB does. The church's doctrine of the Trinity was formed without it and does not depend on it.
cultural:
Testimony (martyria) was a legal idea in both Jewish and Roman settings. The law of Moses required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), and John draws on that principle: the Spirit, the water, and the blood are three witnesses in agreement. If human courts accept human testimony, how much more should God's testimony about his Son be believed.

The final command, keep yourselves from idols, would have had immediate force in a city like Ephesus, whose temple of Artemis was one of the wonders of the ancient world, and where images of gods and emperors filled streets, homes, and marketplaces. Trade guilds held meals in honor of patron deities, and civic life was full of sacrifice. John's warning may also be broader, reaching any false image of God, including the false Christ of the teachers who had left. Either way, it is a fitting last word: after telling his readers who the true God is, John warns them against every substitute.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-12 form a closely linked chain of argument, each clause building on the last: believing, being born of God, loving, obeying, overcoming, testifying, having life. The word testimony and its verb dominate verses 6-11. Verse 13 is the letter's purpose statement and begins the conclusion. Verses 14-21 turn to prayer and then to three solemn statements that each begin with we know (verses 18, 19, 20), a summary of the letter's assurance. The last verse is abrupt, a single command with no farewell, which gives it the force of a final charge. The whole letter is framed by eternal life (1:2 and 5:20).

outline.t: Faith, love, and obedience overcome the world
The testimony of the Spirit, the water, and the blood
Assurance of life and confidence in prayer
What we know, and a final warning against idols

doctrines.note: Faith that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, is the victory that overcomes the world (verse 4). It is not a leap in the dark but a response to God's own testimony about his Son.
God has given eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life (verses 11-12), and believers may know, not merely hope, that they have it.
Believers pray with confidence, knowing that God hears requests made according to his will, including prayer for a brother or sister caught in sin (verses 14-16).
The letter ends by warning against idols. Having named Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life, John calls believers to guard against anything, visible or doctrinal, that would take his place.

words.note: Martyria, testimony or witness, used six times in the chapter. It carries a legal sense: evidence given to establish the truth. John's argument is that God has given his own testimony about his Son, and to refuse it is to call God a liar. The related word martys later came to mean a martyr, one whose death bears witness.

Nikao, to conquer or overcome, from the same root as Nike, the Greek goddess of victory. John uses it for the believer's victory over the world. The victory is not military or political but the triumph of faith in the Son of God over a world that does not know him.
Eidolon, idol, an image of a god, and more broadly any false object of worship. It is the letter's last word in Greek. Having shown who the true God is, John warns against all counterfeits.

christ: The chapter confesses Jesus as the Christ and the Son of God, the one who came by water and blood, fully sharing human life and truly dying. God's testimony centers on him, and eternal life is found in him and nowhere else. Verse 18 speaks of the One who was born of God, most likely Christ himself, who keeps believers safe so that the evil one cannot touch them. Verse 20 says that the Son of God has come and given understanding so that we may know him who is true, and then states: He is the true God and eternal life. Grammarians debate whether He refers to the Son or to the Father, but many interpreters, noting that the nearest antecedent is Jesus Christ and that the letter began by calling him the eternal life, read it as a clear confession of Christ's deity.

hard.q: What is the sin that leads to death, and why doesn't John tell us to pray about it?
hard.a:
John does not define it, and interpreters have offered several readings. Some take it as sin that leads to physical death as a divine judgment, as with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5) or the Corinthians who were sick and died (1 Corinthians 11:30). Others take it as a deliberate, final rejection of Christ, the kind shown by those who left the community and denied the Son, which puts a person outside the source of life. Some connect it with Jesus' warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The Old Testament distinction between unintentional sins and sins committed defiantly (Numbers 15:27-31) may also lie in the background.

Many interpreters think the context points to the second reading, since the letter's whole concern is with those who denied that Jesus is the Christ. Note what John does and doesn't say. He does not forbid praying for such a person; he simply does not command it. His emphasis is positive: pray for the brother or sister who is sinning, and God will give life. The passage is meant to encourage intercession, not to make anxious believers wonder whether they have committed an unforgivable sin. The very fear of having done so is usually a sign that one has not rejected Christ.

questions: John says that God's commands are not burdensome. When have you experienced obedience as freedom rather than weight?
John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life. What makes that kind of assurance hard for you, and where does John point you for it?
What idols, visible or invisible, are most likely to take the place of the true God in your life or community?
